error_modes.label: Knowledge and selection of the correct visual signal

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published visual signal set, did not know and execute the correct signal for the required action and passed signals that meant a different maneuver to the other member. On three separate occasions the wrong signal was given and the formation started an action that had not been briefed, so IP took over the direction of the flight by radio for the remainder of the sortie. The requirement to know and execute all visual signals was not met and IP intervention was required.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published visual signal set, selected the wrong signal for the intended action twice and did not recognize the error unaided. The correct signal was passed only after IP prompted verbally on each occasion, and the formation action was delayed by about ten seconds each time. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because no self-correction occurred.
texts.2: SP, due to incomplete recall of the less frequently used signals, started the wrong hand signal for the fuel check. SP recognized the error without prompting, cancelled the signal and passed the correct one within about three seconds, and the flight continued as briefed. The action was completed correctly with timely self-correction and no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP knew and executed the correct visual signal for every required action throughout the sortie. Each signal matched the published set and conveyed the intended maneuver to the other member without ambiguity. No improvised signals were used and no radio backup was needed.
texts.4: SP demonstrated complete command of the visual signal set, including the rarely used signals, and selected the correct one instantly in every case. Signals were passed with no hesitation and matched the published standard exactly. The other member acted on each signal without a single request for clarification.
texts.marginal: SP knew and executed the correct visual signals within standards, but selection of the less common signals followed a visible pause on two occasions. The pause is a trend towards hesitation on signals outside the routine set. SP is expected to review the complete signal list before the next sortie so that recall of every signal is immediate.

error_modes.label: Signal conspicuity and duration - perceivable beyond doubt

texts.0: SP, due to hand movement kept low inside the cockpit and below the canopy rail, did not execute the signals in a way perceivable beyond doubt from the other aircraft. Four consecutive signals went unseen by the other member, the flight stayed in the previous configuration, and IP had to take over and pass the direction by radio. The requirement for signals perceivable beyond doubt was not met and IP intervention was required.
texts.1: SP, due to signals given with a small rapid hand movement held for under one second, did not make them perceivable beyond doubt from the other aircraft. The other member did not react until IP directed SP verbally to repeat each signal larger and hold it, which happened on three signals. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the presentation was corrected only after prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial signal given with the hand partly masked by the canopy bow, was not seen immediately by the other member. SP recognized the absence of a response, repositioned the hand into clear view and held the signal until acknowledged, all within about two seconds and without prompting. The signal was made perceivable by timely self-correction with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed every signal high in the canopy with a deliberate and exaggerated movement and held it until it was acknowledged. All signals were perceivable beyond doubt from the other member's position and none required repetition.
texts.4: SP presented every signal at exactly the right size, position and duration for the formation geometry flown, adapting the presentation to the other member's line of sight in echelon and in route. No signal required repetition or clarification at any point in the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP made the signals perceivable within standards, but two of them were held only just long enough for the other member to read them. The trend is towards short signal duration that leaves no margin if the other member is momentarily cross-checking. SP is expected to hold each signal until the acknowledgment is seen on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Acknowledgment of signals addressed to the SP

texts.0: SP, due to lack of communication of the recognized signal back to the originator, did not confirm with a visual signal that the signals addressed to SP had been understood. Five signals from the leader were left unacknowledged, the leader repeated each of them and finally reverted to radio, and IP intervened to direct the acknowledgment. The requirement to confirm understanding by visual signal was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on maintaining the briefed position, did not return the confirming signal for three of the leader's signals. Each confirmation was passed only after IP directed SP verbally, about eight seconds after the original signal. Performance stayed at the limit of the standard because acknowledgment came only after prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to the head being briefly inside the cockpit when the signal was passed, did not acknowledge the leader's signal at first. SP saw the repeated signal, returned the confirming signal within about two seconds and then executed the directed action, with no prompting from IP. Confirmation was restored by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP confirmed with a clear visual signal that every signal addressed to SP had been understood, before starting the directed action. Each acknowledgment was returned promptly and the leader never had to repeat a signal.
texts.4: SP acknowledged every signal received immediately and unambiguously, and where the signal called for a specific response SP returned the matching signal rather than a generic acknowledgment. The originator was left in no doubt about SP's understanding at any point in the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP confirmed understanding of the signals addressed to SP within standards, but on two occasions the acknowledgment was returned only after the directed action had already started. The trend is towards acting first and confirming afterwards, which leaves the originator briefly uncertain. SP is expected to acknowledge before initiating the directed action on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Interpretation of signals received from the other member

texts.0: SP did not apprehend the signals passed by the other member and read the fuel check signal as the signal for a lead change. SP moved forward out of the briefed position while the leader was still maneuvering, the flight lost its briefed geometry, and IP took control to reposition the aircraft. The requirement to apprehend the visual signals was not met and IP intervention was required.
texts.1: SP misread two of the leader's signals and started the wrong action on each occasion. SP stopped and applied the correct action only after IP explained the meaning of the signal verbally, delaying the formation action by about fifteen seconds each time. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the misreading was not resolved by SP.
texts.2: SP initially misread the leader's signal for the configuration change and began to select the wrong control. SP compared the signal with the briefed sequence, corrected the interpretation within about three seconds and completed the correct action, with no IP intervention. The error was contained by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP apprehended every signal passed by the other member correctly and executed the directed action without hesitation. No signal was misread and no clarification was requested at any point in the sortie.
texts.4: SP read every signal correctly at first presentation, including signals given in echelon where the presentation angle was less favorable. Each directed action followed immediately and exactly as briefed, with no verbal backup at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP apprehended the signals within standards, but on two occasions there was a noticeable delay before the meaning was acted upon. The trend is towards reading the signal correctly only after a second look. SP is expected to build immediate recognition so that interpretation and action are continuous.

error_modes.label: Timing and sequencing of signals within the maneuver

texts.0: SP, due to signals passed without regard to the phase of the maneuver, gave the configuration signal while the formation was established in a turn and the other member was working to hold position. The signal was passed at a point where it could not be read, the flight ended up in split configurations, and IP intervened to restore a common configuration by radio. The signals were not executed in a way that was usable by the other member of the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to signals passed before the formation was steady, gave three of them during unstable phases when the other member could not read them. SP re-timed the signals only after IP directed verbally to wait for wings level, and each formation action was delayed by about twenty seconds. Performance stayed at the limit of the standard because the timing was corrected only with prompting.
texts.2: SP started the descent signal just as the formation entered a turn. SP recognized that the other member's attention was on holding position, held the signal until wings level and then passed it, without prompting from IP. The signal was delivered effectively with timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP passed each signal at the correct point in the sequence, waiting for a steady formation and allowing the other member time to read, acknowledge and act before the maneuver began. The timing of every signal supported the briefed sequence.
texts.4: SP timed every signal precisely to the phase of flight, anticipating the point at which the other member could read it and leaving exactly the right interval before the action. The formation flowed through the briefed sequence with no pause and no repeated signal at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP timed the signals within standards, but twice the signal was passed with only a small margin before the action was required. The trend is towards late signalling that compresses the other member's reaction time. SP is expected to pass each signal earlier so that there is time to acknowledge and prepare.

error_modes.label: Aircraft control and lookout while giving or reading signals

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on presenting the hand signal at the expense of the outside scan, did not maintain the briefed position while executing the signals. Formation spacing opened well beyond the briefed limits and then closed unpredictably during each signal, and IP took control to re-establish a safe position. Executing the visual signals cost SP aircraft control and required IP intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to attention concentrated on the hand signal, allowed the formation position to drift each time a signal was passed. SP returned to the briefed position only after IP prompted verbally, on three occasions. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the position was recovered only with prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to presenting the signal, allowed a small step-down and spacing deviation while the signal was held. SP detected the drift, returned to the briefed position within about three seconds and completed the signal, with no prompting and no IP intervention. The deviation was contained by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP executed and read the visual signals while holding the briefed position and maintaining the outside scan. Signalling never cost SP aircraft control and clearing continued throughout the sortie.
texts.4: SP passed and read every signal with no detectable effect on formation position or lookout. The scan, the position cross-check and the signalling ran together smoothly and the other aircraft was kept in sight at all times.
texts.marginal: SP kept position and lookout within standards while signalling, but a small position deviation appeared on each of the longer signals. The trend is towards attention being drawn inside while the hand signal is held. SP is expected to keep the position cross-check running through the signal on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Visual signals exchanged with the tower and ground personnel

texts.0: SP did not know and execute the visual signals exchanged with the tower and with ground personnel. SP did not respond to the light signal directed at the aircraft and did not acknowledge the marshaller's instructions, so IP took over the coordination with the tower and the ground crew. The requirement to execute and apprehend the visual signals with the tower was not met and IP intervention was required.
texts.1: SP recognized the tower light signal but did not know the required response and gave no acknowledgment. The correct response was passed only after IP directed SP verbally, about ten seconds after the signal was given. Performance stayed at the limit of the standard because no self-correction occurred.
texts.2: SP initially misread the marshaller's signal and started the wrong ground action. SP rechecked the signal, corrected within about two seconds and complied as directed, with no IP intervention. Coordination with ground personnel was restored by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP executed and apprehended every visual signal exchanged with the tower and with ground personnel correctly and acknowledged each one in the prescribed way. No signal originating outside the formation was missed or misread.
texts.4: SP responded to every tower and ground visual signal immediately and with the exact prescribed acknowledgment, including the signals used only in the lost communications case. Coordination with the tower and the ground crew was complete with no verbal backup required.
texts.marginal: SP handled the tower and ground visual signals within standards, but the acknowledgment to the marshaller was given only after a second look on two occasions. The trend is towards delayed recognition of signals originating outside the formation. SP is expected to include the tower and ground signal set in the pre-flight review.

error_modes.label: Signal proportional to range - wing rock and wing dip sizing

texts.0: SP, due to visual signals that were not proportional to range, passed a slight wing rock as the reform signal while the other member was at 500-foot route spacing. The signal could not be read from that distance and was repeated three times unchanged, the formation stayed split for over a minute, and IP took over the direction of the flight and reformed the pair by radio. The requirement for signals perceivable beyond doubt was not met and IP intervention was required.
texts.1: SP, due to a wing rock sized for close spacing while the other member was well out in route, did not scale the signal to the distance between the aircraft. IP directed SP verbally to repeat the signal larger on three occasions before the other member reacted, and each reform was delayed by about fifteen seconds. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the signal size was corrected only after prompting.
texts.2: SP started the reform wing rock at a size suited to two ship-width route while the other member was further out. SP saw no acknowledgment, immediately increased the amplitude of the wing rock to match the actual spacing and had the signal read within about three seconds, without prompting. The signal was made proportional to range by timely self-correction with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP sized every visual signal in proportion to the range between the aircraft, using a slight wing rock to reform from two ship-width route and a large wing rock from the wider route positions. Each signal was read at the first presentation and none had to be repeated. The crossunder wing dip was likewise sized to the other member's spacing.
texts.4: SP judged the range to the other member accurately before every signal and sized the wing rock and the wing dip exactly to that spacing throughout the sortie. No signal was so large that it disturbed the flight path and none was too small to be read. Every signal was acknowledged on the first presentation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the visual signals proportional to range within standards, but two wing rocks passed from the wider route positions were only just large enough to be read. The trend is towards sizing signals for close spacing regardless of the actual range. SP is expected to assess the distance to the other member before each signal on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Acknowledging or changing position when unsure of a signal

texts.0: SP, unsure of a signal passed by the other member, acknowledged it with a head nod and changed position instead of withholding the acknowledgment. The aircraft was repositioned on the wrong side while the leader was still expecting the previous geometry, this happened twice in the sortie, and IP took control to restore the briefed position. The rule that an unsure wingman neither acknowledges nor changes position was not applied.
texts.1: SP, unsure of two signals received, returned an acknowledgment anyway rather than leaving the signal unacknowledged so that it would be repeated. On both occasions IP directed SP verbally to stop the movement and query the other member before any repositioning took place. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because SP acknowledged a signal that had not been understood.
texts.2: SP began a head nod for a signal that had not been fully read and started to move towards the new position. SP recognized the doubt at once, stopped the movement within about two seconds, withheld the acknowledgment and waited for the signal to be repeated, all without prompting. The correct response to an unclear signal was restored by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP acknowledged only the signals that had been read beyond doubt and withheld the acknowledgment on the one signal that was unclear, holding position until it was repeated. No position change was made on the basis of a signal that had not been understood.
texts.4: SP applied the rule consistently, acknowledging only what was understood and holding position on any doubtful signal until it was repeated or clarified. On the single ambiguous signal of the sortie SP withheld the head nod, kept the briefed position and had the signal repeated within two seconds. No unnecessary movement resulted.
texts.marginal: SP withheld the acknowledgment on unclear signals within standards, but on one occasion the head nod was returned while SP was still working out the meaning of the signal. The trend is towards acknowledging early and resolving the doubt afterwards. SP is expected to read a signal fully before returning any acknowledgment on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Only the pilot at the controls gives or acknowledges signals

texts.0: SP, while not the pilot at the controls, gave visual signals to the other aircraft and acknowledged signals received from it. The other member acted on signals that did not come from the pilot flying, the flight changed configuration on an unintended cue on two occasions, and IP took control to stop the exchange and re-establish who was signalling. The rule that only the pilot at the controls signals another aircraft was not applied.
texts.1: SP, not being the pilot at the controls, started the signalling to the other aircraft on three occasions instead of leaving it to the pilot flying. Each time IP directed SP verbally to stop and let the pilot at the controls pass the signal. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the correct allocation of the signalling role was restored only after prompting.
texts.2: SP raised a hand to acknowledge a signal from the other aircraft while the controls were with the other pilot. SP recognized the role error within about two seconds, lowered the hand before the signal could be read from outside and passed the information internally so that the pilot at the controls could acknowledge. No confusion reached the other member and no prompting was required.
texts.3: SP gave and acknowledged visual signals to the other aircraft only while at the controls, and left the exchange entirely to the pilot flying at all other times. The other member always received the signals from the correct source and no duplicate or conflicting signal was passed.
texts.4: SP kept the signalling role tied to the controls throughout the sortie, including across two transfers of control, and confirmed the change of role each time. Every signal seen by the other member originated from the pilot at the controls, with no duplication and no ambiguity about who was directing the formation.
texts.marginal: SP kept the signalling with the pilot at the controls within standards, but after one transfer of control SP acknowledged a signal before the change of role had settled. The trend is towards signalling out of role immediately after a change of controls. SP is expected to confirm who is at the controls before giving or acknowledging any signal on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Radio used to clear up confusion and in place of signals in IMC

texts.0: SP, persisting with visual signals after the exchange had clearly broken down, did not use the radio to immediately clear up the confusion. Four repetitions of the same signal were passed without a common understanding, and the configuration change was directed by visual signal after entering cloud, where a radio call is required. The formation ended up in split configuration on the approach and IP took over the communications for the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to transmit when a visual signal was not understood, kept repeating the signal instead of using the radio. The confusion persisted for about twenty seconds on two occasions and was resolved only after IP directed SP verbally to make the radio call. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the radio backup came only after prompting.
texts.2: SP repeated a visual signal twice with no acknowledgment as the visibility deteriorated. SP recognized that the signal was no longer readable, transmitted a short radio call within about three seconds and cleared the confusion immediately, without prompting. The change to the radio was made in time and no configuration or position error followed.
texts.3: SP used the radio without delay whenever a visual signal was not understood, and used a radio call rather than a visual signal for the configuration change flown in instrument conditions. No misunderstanding was allowed to persist and the flight was never left with an unresolved signal.
texts.4: SP judged the point at which a visual signal ceased to be reliable before any confusion developed and moved to the radio each time with a short, correctly formatted call. Configuration changes in instrument conditions were directed by radio only, and every visual exchange in visual conditions was resolved without needing the radio at all.
texts.marginal: SP used the radio to clear up confusion within standards, but on two occasions the call was made only after the visual signal had been repeated three times. The trend is towards holding on to the visual exchange longer than the conditions support. SP is expected to move to the radio after the second unacknowledged signal on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Lead change by visual signal - expedition and acknowledgment

texts.0: SP, treating the lead change as complete before the head nod was returned, gave up the lead on a visual signal that the other member had not acknowledged. Neither aircraft was actively clearing for the formation for about thirty seconds, both flew as wingman through the following turn, and IP took control to re-establish who was leading. The requirement that the lead change is complete only on acknowledgment was not met.
texts.1: SP conducted the lead changes with visual signals so slowly that the flight was left without a leader actively clearing for about twenty seconds on each of two changes. IP prompted SP verbally each time to complete the signal and obtain the acknowledgment. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the exchange was expedited only after prompting.
texts.2: SP passed the lead change signal and started to relinquish the lead before the head nod had been seen. SP recognized that no acknowledgment had been returned, continued to lead and clear for a further three seconds until the head nod appeared, and only then transferred the lead. The transfer was completed correctly by timely self-correction with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the lead change signal expeditiously and considered the change complete only after the head nod was returned. The formation was never left without a leader actively clearing and the new roles were unambiguous to both aircraft.
texts.4: SP passed the lead change signal, obtained the acknowledgment and completed the transfer in one continuous sequence, keeping the time without a leader actively clearing to a minimum. Both aircraft were clear about the new roles from the moment of the head nod, and the new leader set a power setting that let the new wingman move into position without difficulty.
texts.marginal: SP completed the lead changes on acknowledgment and within standards, but the visual exchange took noticeably longer than the briefed sequence on one occasion. The trend is towards a slow signal exchange that extends the time without a leader actively clearing for the formation. SP is expected to tighten the signal and acknowledgment sequence on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: No radio operation - wing rock for attention in the air

texts.0: SP, following the simulated total radio failure, did not rock the wings for attention in the air and did not show the appropriate visual signal after moving out of fingertip. SP then closed inside route position without being directed, arriving in fingertip while the other member was still unaware of the failure, and IP took control to separate the aircraft. The visual procedure for a no radio aircraft was not applied.
texts.1: SP, after the simulated radio failure, rocked the wings only after IP prompted verbally and then began to close on the other member before any signal had been returned. On both occasions IP directed SP verbally to hold no closer than route position until directed. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the no radio visual procedure was applied only after prompting.
texts.2: SP started to close inside route position after the simulated radio failure before a rejoin had been directed. SP recognized the error within about three seconds, stopped the closure at route spacing, rocked the wings to attract attention and showed the appropriate signal, without prompting. The correct no radio geometry was restored by timely self-correction.
texts.3: SP handled the simulated radio failure entirely by visual signals, moving out of fingertip, rocking the wings for attention in the air and showing the appropriate signal. SP held no closer than route position until directed and then complied with each subsequent visual direction.
texts.4: SP recognized the simulated radio failure immediately, moved smoothly out of fingertip, attracted attention with a correctly sized wing rock and passed the appropriate signal at the first attempt. SP held route position throughout and closed only on a clear visual direction, and the visual signal passing the landing clearance was read and acted on without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP flew the simulated no radio profile within standards, but on one rejoin SP was already drifting inside route spacing as the direction to close was given. The trend is towards anticipating the direction instead of waiting for it. SP is expected to hold route position until the signal is unmistakably given on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Head nod sequence gating run-up and brake release on takeoff

texts.0: SP, fixating inside the cockpit during the run-up, did not see the run-up signal and did not return the head nod that signifies ready for takeoff. SP then released the brakes without the downward head nod, the two aircraft started the roll about two seconds apart and the formation takeoff geometry was lost, so IP took control on the runway. The head nod sequence that gates the formation takeoff was not followed.
texts.1: SP, with attention held inside the cockpit at the holding point, missed the run-up signal and the ready for takeoff look, and both head nods were returned only after IP prompted verbally. The departure was delayed by about twenty seconds and the sequence had to be restarted from the run-up signal. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the gating signals were given only after prompting.
texts.2: SP looked inside for the engine indications and initially missed the ready for takeoff look from the other aircraft. SP came back outside within about two seconds unprompted, returned the head nod and released the brakes precisely on the downward head nod. The formation started the roll together and no lateral divergence developed.
texts.3: SP gave a head nod to signify ready for run-up, acknowledged the run-up signal with a head nod and released the brakes on the downward head nod. Each signal was returned promptly with the head outside the cockpit and the two aircraft began the takeoff roll together.
texts.4: SP kept the head outside for the whole gating sequence, returning each nod without delay and confirming the engine indications with brief glances only. Brake release matched the downward head nod exactly, the aircraft did not creep forward during the run-up and the formation accelerated as a pair from the start of the roll.
texts.marginal: SP followed the head nod sequence for run-up and brake release within standards, but the ready for takeoff nod was returned late once because attention was still inside the cockpit. The trend is towards head down time at the holding point that delays the gating signals. SP is expected to complete the engine check before the other aircraft looks across on the next sortie.

error_modes.label: Thumbs-up as a report of a completed check or verified configuration
error_modes.source: technique:9.27 GROUND OPERATIONS - START, BEFORE TAXI, TAXI, BEFORE TAKEOFF, AFTER LANDING,technique:9.40.2 FORMATION APPROACH,technique:9.8 BATTLE DAMAGE (BD) CHECK

texts.0: SP passed the thumbs-up before the check it reports had been completed, giving the ready to taxi thumbs-up with the before taxi items unfinished and returning the configuration thumbs-up on the approach without looking at the other aircraft's gear and flaps. Both reports were accepted as valid and the formation continued towards the runway with an unverified configuration, so IP intervened and stopped the sequence. The thumbs-up was used as a habit rather than as a report of a verified condition.
texts.1: SP gave the thumbs-up for the completed before takeoff checks and for a clean battle damage check without having inspected the items that the signal reports. IP directed SP verbally on both occasions to complete the check and to repeat the signal only when it was true. Performance remained at the limit of the standard because the reports were made valid only after prompting.
texts.2: SP raised a thumbs-up for the approach configuration before finishing the look at the other aircraft's gear and flaps. SP recognized this within about two seconds, withdrew the signal, checked the configuration properly and then passed the thumbs-up again. The report was made accurate by timely self-correction with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used the thumbs-up only as a report of a condition actually verified, covering readiness to taxi, completion of the before takeoff checks, a clean battle damage check and the other aircraft's approach configuration. Each signal was given after the check behind it was finished and none had to be withdrawn or repeated.
texts.4: SP treated every thumbs-up as a formal report and gave it only after a deliberate check, including a full inspection of the other aircraft before declaring the battle damage check clean. Each signal was passed promptly once the condition was verified, and the one discrepancy noticed was reported by radio in place of the thumbs-up as prescribed.
texts.marginal: SP used the thumbs-up as a report of a verified condition within standards, but the approach configuration thumbs-up was returned after only a brief glance at the other aircraft. The trend is towards passing the report before the check behind it is complete. SP is expected to finish each check before raising the thumbs-up on the next sortie.
